subjects.name: Intel 8086 Microprocessor
subjects.description: Bus demultiplexing, minimum mode, segmentation, memory banking, bus timing cycles, instruction set, addressing modes, stack, CALL/RET, and interrupts.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Bus Demultiplexing & Memory Interfacing
chapters.description: Demultiplexing ALE, 74LS373 latches, 74LS245 transceivers, tristate logic, address decoding, 74LS138, clock timing & bus contention.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Pins, Signals, Internal Architecture & Bus Cycles
chapters.description: BIU & EU, 6-byte instruction queue, pipelining, segment registers, Even/Odd memory banks (BHE/A0), read/write timing cycles, wait state (Tw) & interrupts.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Instruction Set & Addressing Modes
chapters.description: Machine instruction encoding (d, w, mod, reg, r/m), 12 addressing modes, arithmetic/logic, shifts/rotates, strings, and control transfer.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Interrupts, Stack, Subroutines & Strings
chapters.description: Interrupt vector table (IVT), hardware vs software interrupts, stack frame mechanics, CALL/RET nuances, string primitives & shift/rotate flags.

banks.title: 8086 Objective MCQ Bank (258 MCQs)
banks.description: Comprehensive university multiple-choice question bank covering all syllabus topics with verified keys.

banks.title: 8086 True / False Diagnostic Assessment (296 Qs)
banks.description: Exhaustive True/False worksheet testing deep technical understanding, edge-cases, and common traps.

banks.title: 8086 Fill-in-the-Blanks Technical Review (128 Qs)
banks.description: Rapid terminology and architectural parameter completion review.

banks.title: 8086 One-Mark Core Q&A Bank (200 Qs)
banks.description: Concise high-yield single mark definitions, formulas, and pin explanations from Unit 1, Unit 2, and Unit 3.

banks.title: Interrupts, Stack, CALL & RET Pack (36 Qs)
banks.description: Deep-dive questions on IVT, hardware interrupts, stack pointer operations, and subroutines.

banks.title: Shift & Rotate Instructions Pack (27 Qs)
banks.description: SHL, SHR, SAR, ROL, ROR, RCL, RCR flag transformations and arithmetic shifts.

banks.title: String Instruction Primitives Pack (17 Qs)
banks.description: MOVS, CMPS, SCAS, LODS, STOS, direction flag DF, and REP prefixes.

banks.title: 8086 Numerical & 8-Mark Practice Pack (34 Qs)
banks.description: Calculation problems covering physical memory capacity, bus cycle time, contention current, and program traces.

banks.title: Master Question Bank Theory & T/F (75 Qs)
banks.description: COEP End-Sem Master Question Bank MCQs and True/False statements with teacher rationale.

banks.title: Master Numerical Question Bank (45 Qs)
banks.description: Algorithmic numerical problems with step-by-step mathematical decodings.

subjects.name: Principles of Programming Languages
subjects.description: Language evaluation criteria, implementation models (compilers, interpreters, JVM), formal syntax/semantics, control statements, subprograms, exception handling, and paradigms.

chapters.title: Unit 1: Programming Language Concepts
chapters.description: Reasons for study, language evaluation criteria (readability, writability, reliability, cost), expressive power, orthogonality, and domain suitability.

chapters.title: Unit 2: Language Implementation Methods
chapters.description: Compilers, interpreters, hybrid implementations, bytecode, JIT compilation, virtual machines (JVM), linkers, loaders, and environments.

chapters.title: Unit 3: Syntax, Semantics & Lexical Analysis
chapters.description: Grammars, BNF, EBNF, parse trees, ambiguity, operator precedence, associativity, attribute grammars, lexical analysis, and tokens.

chapters.title: Unit 4: Statement Control & Subprograms
chapters.description: Selection statements, iterative statements, control flow, parameter passing methods (pass-by-value, pass-by-reference), and scoping rules.

chapters.title: Unit 5: Exception, Event & GUI Handling
chapters.description: Exception handling architectures, try/catch/finally, propagation, event-driven programming, listeners, and GUI frameworks.

chapters.title: Unit 6: Programming Paradigms
chapters.description: Imperative vs declarative, functional programming (Haskell, Lisp), logic programming (Prolog), object-oriented programming (Java, C++), and scripting.

banks.title: PPL Complete Syllabus Question Bank (240 Qs)
banks.description: 120 MCQs and 120 high-yield concept Q&As covering all 6 units with complete solutions.

banks.title: PPL Mid-Sem Exam High-Yield Bank (38 Qs)
banks.description: Mid-sem targeted MCQs and Right/Wrong diagnostics with explanations.

questions.explanation: S₇ is a spare status bit combined with BHE during T₂–T₄ (currently unused/reserved).

questions.question: What is the function of the RD signal?
questions.answerText: RD (Read) indicates that the CPU is performing a memory or I/O read operation.
questions.explanation: RD (Read) indicates that the CPU is performing a memory or I/O read operation.

questions.question: Is RD active high or active low?
questions.explanation: RD is an active-low signal.

questions.question: What is the function of the RESET pin?
questions.answerText: RESET causes the processor to immediately terminate present activity and restart execution from CS:IP = FFFF:0000H.
questions.explanation: RESET causes the processor to immediately terminate present activity and restart execution from CS:IP = FFFF:0000H.

questions.question: What type of interrupt is NMI?
questions.answerText: NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt) is a hardware interrupt that cannot be masked or disabled by software.
questions.explanation: NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt) is a hardware interrupt that cannot be masked or disabled by software.

questions.question: What type of interrupt is INTR?
questions.answerText: INTR (Interrupt Request) is a maskable hardware interrupt controlled by the Interrupt Flag (IF).
questions.explanation: INTR (Interrupt Request) is a maskable hardware interrupt controlled by the Interrupt Flag (IF).

questions.question: What is the function of CLK?
questions.answerText: CLK provides the basic timing signal for processor operations.
questions.explanation: CLK provides the basic timing signal for processor operations.

questions.question: What is the function of VCC?
questions.answerText: VCC supplies power (+5V DC) to the microprocessor chip.
questions.explanation: VCC supplies power (+5V DC) to the microprocessor chip.

questions.question: What is the function of GND?
questions.answerText: GND provides the ground reference voltage (0V) for the processor.
questions.explanation: GND provides the ground reference voltage (0V) for the processor.

questions.question: What is the function of READY?
questions.answerText: READY is an input signal from slow memory or I/O devices indicating data is ready, inserting Wait states if low.
questions.explanation: READY is an input signal from slow memory or I/O devices indicating data is ready, inserting Wait states if low.

questions.question: What is the function of TEST?
questions.answerText: TEST is examined by the WAIT instruction; if TEST is high, CPU waits until TEST becomes low.
questions.explanation: TEST is examined by the WAIT instruction; if TEST is high, CPU waits until TEST becomes low.

questions.question: What is the function of MN/MX?
questions.answerText: MN/MX selects Minimum Mode when connected to VCC and Maximum Mode when connected to GND.
questions.explanation: MN/MX selects Minimum Mode when connected to VCC and Maximum Mode when connected to GND.

questions.question: Which signals indicate the segment accessed during a bus cycle?
questions.answerText: Status signals S₄ and S₃ indicate the segment register accessed during a bus cycle.
questions.explanation: Status signals S₄ and S₃ indicate the segment register accessed during a bus cycle.

questions.question: What segment is indicated by S4S3 = 00?
questions.answerText: S₄S₃ = 00 indicates Extra Segment (ES) access (or Alternate Data).
questions.explanation: S₄S₃ = 00 indicates Extra Segment (ES) access (or Alternate Data).

questions.question: What segment is indicated by S4S3 = 01?
questions.explanation: S₄S₃ = 01 indicates Stack Segment (SS) access.

questions.question: What segment is indicated by S4S3 = 10?
questions.answerText: S₄S₃ = 10 indicates Code Segment (CS) access (or no segment access).
questions.explanation: S₄S₃ = 10 indicates Code Segment (CS) access (or no segment access).

questions.question: What segment is indicated by S4S3 = 11?
questions.explanation: S₄S₃ = 11 indicates Data Segment (DS) access.

questions.question: What does S5 indicate?
questions.answerText: S₅ reflects the current state of the Interrupt Enable Flag (IF).
questions.explanation: S₅ reflects the current state of the Interrupt Enable Flag (IF).

questions.question: What does a low level on S6 indicate?
questions.answerText: A low level on S₆ indicates that 8086 is controlling the bus (S₆ is always held low by 8086).
questions.explanation: A low level on S₆ indicates that 8086 is controlling the bus (S₆ is always held low by 8086).

questions.question: What does BHE become after T1?
questions.answerText: After T₁, the BHE pin multiplexes to output status bit S₇ during T₂, T₃, T₄.
questions.explanation: After T₁, the BHE pin multiplexes to output status bit S₇ during T₂, T₃, T₄.

questions.question: What does S7 indicate during subsequent T-states?
questions.answerText: S₇ is a spare status signal (currently undefined / logic 1).
questions.explanation: S₇ is a spare status signal (currently undefined / logic 1).

questions.question: How are BHE and A0 used together?
questions.answerText: BHE and A₀ are decoded together to determine byte or word transfers across even/odd memory banks (BHE=0, A₀=0: Whole Word transfer; BHE=0, A₀=1: Upper Byte from odd bank; BHE=1, A₀=0: Lower Byte from even bank).
questions.explanation: BHE and A₀ are decoded together to determine byte or word transfers across even/odd memory banks (BHE=0, A₀=0: Whole Word transfer; BHE=0, A₀=1: Upper Byte from odd bank; BHE=1, A₀=0: Lower Byte from even bank).

questions.question: For how long is RESET held high for power-on reset according to the notes?
questions.answerText: For power-on reset, RESET must be held high for at least 50 microseconds.
questions.explanation: For power-on reset, RESET must be held high for at least 50 microseconds.

questions.question: For how many clock cycles is RESET held high during a working reset?
questions.answerText: During normal running operations, RESET must be held high for at least 4 clock cycles.
questions.explanation: During normal running operations, RESET must be held high for at least 4 clock cycles.

questions.question: What happens to the instruction queue during reset?
questions.answerText: The instruction queue is cleared / flushed during reset.
questions.explanation: The instruction queue is cleared / flushed during reset.

questions.question: What is the value loaded into CS after reset?
questions.answerText: Code Segment register CS is loaded with FFFFH after reset.
questions.explanation: Code Segment register CS is loaded with FFFFH after reset.

questions.question: What is the initial physical address fetched after reset?
questions.answerText: The initial physical address fetched is FFFFFH (calculated from CS:IP = FFFF0H + 0000H).
questions.explanation: The initial physical address fetched is FFFFFH (calculated from CS:IP = FFFF0H + 0000H).

questions.question: What happens to DS during reset?
questions.answerText: Data Segment register DS is cleared to 0000H during reset.
questions.explanation: Data Segment register DS is cleared to 0000H during reset.

questions.question: What happens to SS during reset?
questions.answerText: Stack Segment register SS is cleared to 0000H during reset.
questions.explanation: Stack Segment register SS is cleared to 0000H during reset.

questions.question: What happens to ES during reset?
questions.answerText: Extra Segment register ES is cleared to 0000H during reset.
questions.explanation: Extra Segment register ES is cleared to 0000H during reset.

questions.question: What happens to IP during reset?
questions.answerText: Instruction Pointer IP is cleared to 0000H during reset.
questions.explanation: Instruction Pointer IP is cleared to 0000H during reset.

questions.question: What happens to the flag register during reset?
questions.answerText: The Flag Register is cleared to 0000H (disabling interrupts, single-step, etc.).
questions.explanation: The Flag Register is cleared to 0000H (disabling interrupts, single-step, etc.).

questions.question: What is the purpose of READY?
questions.answerText: READY synchronizes slow memory or I/O devices with the fast CPU by signaling whether data transfer is complete.
questions.explanation: READY synchronizes slow memory or I/O devices with the fast CPU by signaling whether data transfer is complete.

questions.question: When is READY sampled by 8086?
questions.answerText: READY is sampled during clock cycle T₃ (or previous wait state T_w).
questions.explanation: READY is sampled during clock cycle T₃ (or previous wait state T_w).

questions.question: What happens if READY is low?
questions.answerText: If READY is low, the CPU inserts Wait states (T_w) into the bus cycle and pauses execution.
questions.explanation: If READY is low, the CPU inserts Wait states (T_w) into the bus cycle and pauses execution.

questions.question: When does the processor resume from wait states?
questions.answerText: The processor resumes normal bus operations when READY goes high.
questions.explanation: The processor resumes normal bus operations when READY goes high.

questions.question: What logic level is applied to MN/MX for minimum mode?
questions.answerText: High logic level (+5V / VCC) is applied to MN/MX for minimum mode.
questions.explanation: High logic level (+5V / VCC) is applied to MN/MX for minimum mode.

questions.question: Who generates bus-control signals in minimum mode?
questions.answerText: The 8086 microprocessor itself generates all bus-control signals directly in minimum mode.
questions.explanation: The 8086 microprocessor itself generates all bus-control signals directly in minimum mode.

questions.question: What does DT/R stand for?
questions.answerText: DT/R stands for Data Transmit / Receive.
questions.explanation: DT/R stands for Data Transmit / Receive.

questions.question: What is the function of DT/R?
questions.answerText: DT/R controls direction of data flow through external transceivers (High = Transmit/Write, Low = Receive/Read).
questions.explanation: DT/R controls direction of data flow through external transceivers (High = Transmit/Write, Low = Receive/Read).

questions.question: What does DEN stand for?
questions.explanation: DEN stands for Data Enable.

questions.question: What is the function of DEN?
questions.answerText: DEN is an active-low output signal that enables external data bus transceivers (buffers).
questions.explanation: DEN is an active-low output signal that enables external data bus transceivers (buffers).

questions.question: What does ALE stand for?
questions.answerText: ALE stands for Address Latch Enable.
questions.explanation: ALE stands for Address Latch Enable.

questions.question: What is the function of ALE?
questions.answerText: ALE is a high pulse generated during T₁ to strobe memory addresses into external latches (e.g., 8282).
questions.explanation: ALE is a high pulse generated during T₁ to strobe memory addresses into external latches (e.g., 8282).

questions.question: What is the function of M/IO?
questions.answerText: M/IO distinguishes memory accesses (High) from I/O accesses (Low).
questions.explanation: M/IO distinguishes memory accesses (High) from I/O accesses (Low).

questions.question: What is the function of WR?
questions.answerText: WR (Write) indicates that the CPU is writing data to memory or an I/O device.
questions.explanation: WR (Write) indicates that the CPU is writing data to memory or an I/O device.

questions.question: When is WR asserted low?
questions.answerText: WR is asserted low during T₂ and T₃ of a write bus cycle when valid data is present on the data bus.
questions.explanation: WR is asserted low during T₂ and T₃ of a write bus cycle when valid data is present on the data bus.

questions.question: What does HOLD indicate?
questions.answerText: HOLD is an input signal requesting the microprocessor to relinquish control of system buses.
questions.explanation: HOLD is an input signal requesting the microprocessor to relinquish control of system buses.

questions.question: What does HLDA stand for?
questions.explanation: HLDA stands for Hold Acknowledge.

questions.question: What is the function of HLDA?
questions.answerText: HLDA is an output signal acknowledging that the CPU has accepted HOLD and placed bus lines in High-Z.
questions.explanation: HLDA is an output signal acknowledging that the CPU has accepted HOLD and placed bus lines in High-Z.

questions.question: What happens to tristate pins when HOLD is accepted?
questions.answerText: Address, data, and control pins are driven into the High-Impedance (Hi-Z) state.
questions.explanation: Address, data, and control pins are driven into the High-Impedance (Hi-Z) state.

questions.question: What is the relationship between HOLD and HLDA?
questions.answerText: HOLD is the bus request input from an external bus master, and HLDA is the CPU's output confirmation signal.
questions.explanation: HOLD is the bus request input from an external bus master, and HLDA is the CPU's output confirmation signal.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a bidirectional data buffer?
questions.answerText: A bidirectional data buffer (transceiver e.g., 8286) isolates and amplifies signal drive capability on the data bus.
questions.explanation: A bidirectional data buffer (transceiver e.g., 8286) isolates and amplifies signal drive capability on the data bus.

questions.question: What type of architecture does 8086 use?
questions.answerText: 8086 uses a pipelined architecture split into two independent functional units (BIU and EU).
questions.explanation: 8086 uses a pipelined architecture split into two independent functional units (BIU and EU).

questions.question: What does BIU stand for?

questions.question: What does EU stand for?

questions.question: What is the main function of BIU?
questions.answerText: BIU handles all external bus operations, including fetching instruction bytes, reading/writing memory and I/O operands, and physical address calculation.
questions.explanation: BIU handles all external bus operations, including fetching instruction bytes, reading/writing memory and I/O operands, and physical address calculation.

questions.question: What is the main function of EU?
questions.answerText: EU decodes fetched instructions, executes arithmetic and logical operations, and manages general registers and flags.
questions.explanation: EU decodes fetched instructions, executes arithmetic and logical operations, and manages general registers and flags.

questions.question: Do BIU and EU operate independently?
questions.answerText: Yes, BIU and EU operate independently and concurrently in a pipelined fashion.

questions.question: What is the size of the 8086 instruction queue?

questions.question: What is the stack?
questions.answerText:
The stack is the memory area accessed through the Stack Segment register SS and the Stack Pointer SP. It is
used by PUSH and POP and also stores return information for CALL, interrupt entry, and interrupt return.

The stack is the memory area accessed through the Stack Segment register SS and the Stack Pointer SP. It is

A PUSH operation stores a 16-bit quantity, so 2 bytes are pushed. The notes show SP being decremented by 2

questions.question: What is the POP instruction?
questions.answerText:
POP removes the 16-bit value at the top of the stack and transfers it to the specified 16-bit register, segment
register, or memory destination. Afterward SP is increased by 2.
questions.explanation:
POP removes the 16-bit value at the top of the stack and transfers it to the specified 16-bit register, segment
register, or memory destination. Afterward SP is increased by 2.

questions.question: What is the value of SP after a POP instruction?
questions.answerText:
SP becomes two greater than its previous value. In symbolic form: SP <- SP + 2.
Subroutines: CALL and RET
questions.explanation:
SP becomes two greater than its previous value. In symbolic form: SP <- SP + 2.
Subroutines: CALL and RET

questions.question: What is the CALL instruction?
questions.answerText: CALL transfers program control to a procedure or subroutine after saving the return address in the stack memory.
questions.explanation: CALL transfers program control to a procedure or subroutine after saving the return address in the stack memory.

questions.question: In a NEAR CALL instruction, what is pushed onto the stack?
questions.answerText: Only the content of IP, the return offset of the next instruction, is pushed onto the stack.
questions.explanation: Only the content of IP, the return offset of the next instruction, is pushed onto the stack.

questions.question: In a FAR CALL instruction, what is pushed onto the stack?
questions.answerText: Both CS and IP are pushed onto the stack because the called procedure is in a different code segment.
questions.explanation: Both CS and IP are pushed onto the stack because the called procedure is in a different code segment.

questions.question: How many bytes are pushed onto the stack for a NEAR CALL versus a FAR CALL?
questions.answerText:
A near call pushes one 16-bit IP value, so 2 bytes. A far call pushes two 16-bit values, CS and IP, so 4 bytes in
total.
questions.explanation:
A near call pushes one 16-bit IP value, so 2 bytes. A far call pushes two 16-bit values, CS and IP, so 4 bytes in
total.

questions.question:
How is the address of the next instruction stored in IP pushed onto the stack?

8086 Mid-Sem Answer Pack - grounded in the supplied 128-page notes
questions.answerText:
For a near call, SP is first decremented by 2 and the current IP is stored at the new stack top. For a far call, CS is
saved and then IP is saved, each using a 16-bit stack operation.
questions.explanation:
For a near call, SP is first decremented by 2 and the current IP is stored at the new stack top. For a far call, CS is
saved and then IP is saved, each using a 16-bit stack operation.

questions.question: Why is the address of the next instruction pushed onto the stack?
questions.answerText:
It is saved so that RET can later restore the execution point and return control to the calling program after the
subroutine finishes.
questions.explanation:
It is saved so that RET can later restore the execution point and return control to the calling program after the
subroutine finishes.

questions.question: What is the RET instruction?
questions.answerText:
RET returns control from a called procedure to the calling program by taking the saved return information from the
stack.
questions.explanation:
RET returns control from a called procedure to the calling program by taking the saved return information from the
stack.

questions.question: Where are the popped bytes stored, and how are they used?
questions.answerText:
For a near return, the top stack word is popped into IP. For a far return, the top word is loaded into IP and the next
word is loaded into CS. This restores the return address of the calling program.
questions.explanation:
For a near return, the top stack word is popped into IP. For a far return, the top word is loaded into IP and the next
word is loaded into CS. This restores the return address of the calling program.

questions.question: How is IP reloaded to return to the main program in a NEAR return?
questions.answerText: The word at the current top of the stack is moved into IP and SP is incremented by 2.
questions.explanation: The word at the current top of the stack is moved into IP and SP is incremented by 2.

questions.question: How are both CS and IP reloaded to return to the main program in a FAR return?
questions.answerText:
First the top stack word is moved into IP and SP is increased by 2. Then the next stack word is moved into CS
and SP is increased by another 2.
questions.explanation:
First the top stack word is moved into IP and SP is increased by 2. Then the next stack word is moved into CS
and SP is increased by another 2.

questions.question: What is the value of SP after a RET instruction execution?
questions.answerText:
For a near RET, SP is increased by 2. For a far RET, SP is increased by 4 because both IP and CS are restored.
If an immediate-data form of RET is used, the notes also describe an additional increment by the specified value.
Interrupts and IRET
questions.explanation:
For a near RET, SP is increased by 2. For a far RET, SP is increased by 4 because both IP and CS are restored.
If an immediate-data form of RET is used, the notes also describe an additional increment by the specified value.
Interrupts and IRET

questions.question: What is a software interrupt instruction such as INT n?
questions.answerText:
INT is a software interrupt instruction. It calls an interrupt service procedure on an interrupt basis. The type
number n can range from 0 to 255.
questions.explanation:
INT is a software interrupt instruction. It calls an interrupt service procedure on an interrupt basis. The type
number n can range from 0 to 255.

questions.question: What happens when an INT n instruction is executed by the 8086 CPU in a main program?
questions.answerText:
The processor saves the current flag register, CS, and IP on the stack, clears IF and TF, calculates the interrupt
vector address as type x 4, and loads IP and CS from the interrupt vector table so execution can continue from
the interrupt service routine.
questions.explanation:
The processor saves the current flag register, CS, and IP on the stack, clears IF and TF, calculates the interrupt
vector address as type x 4, and loads IP and CS from the interrupt vector table so execution can continue from
the interrupt service routine.

questions.question: In an INT n instruction, what values are pushed onto the stack?
questions.answerText:
The flag register, CS, and IP are pushed onto the stack, in that sequence of interrupt-entry operations, with SP
decremented by 2 before each push.
questions.explanation:
The flag register, CS, and IP are pushed onto the stack, in that sequence of interrupt-entry operations, with SP
decremented by 2 before each push.

questions.question: How many bytes are pushed onto the stack during an INT n instruction?
questions.answerText: Three 16-bit values are saved: FLAGS, CS, and IP. Therefore 6 bytes are pushed in total.
questions.explanation: Three 16-bit values are saved: FLAGS, CS, and IP. Therefore 6 bytes are pushed in total.

questions.question: How is the address of the next instruction pushed onto the stack?
questions.answerText:
The current IP, which points to the next instruction to return to, is stored as a 16-bit stack value after SP is
decremented by 2.
questions.explanation:
The current IP, which points to the next instruction to return to, is stored as a 16-bit stack value after SP is
decremented by 2.

questions.question: Why are the Flags Register, CS, and IP all pushed onto the stack?
questions.answerText:
They preserve the processor state and the exact execution context of the main program so the interrupt service
routine can later return to it. IRET restores IP, CS, and the flags.
questions.explanation:
They preserve the processor state and the exact execution context of the main program so the interrupt service
routine can later return to it. IRET restores IP, CS, and the flags.

questions.question: What is the IRET instruction?
questions.answerText:
IRET terminates the interrupt service routine and returns program control to the interrupted main program by
restoring IP, CS, and the flag register from the stack.
questions.explanation:
IRET terminates the interrupt service routine and returns program control to the interrupted main program by
restoring IP, CS, and the flag register from the stack.

questions.question:
Where are the popped bytes stored, and how are they used?

8086 Mid-Sem Answer Pack - grounded in the supplied 128-page notes
questions.answerText:
IRET loads the top stack word into IP, the next into CS, and the next into the flag register. These values restore
the saved execution context of the interrupted program.
questions.explanation:
IRET loads the top stack word into IP, the next into CS, and the next into the flag register. These values restore
the saved execution context of the interrupted program.

questions.question: How are CS and IP reloaded to return to the main program after an interrupt?
questions.answerText: IRET first pops the saved IP, then the saved CS, and finally the saved flags. SP is increased by 2 after each pop.
questions.explanation: IRET first pops the saved IP, then the saved CS, and finally the saved flags. SP is increased by 2 after each pop.

questions.question: What is the value of SP after an IRET instruction?
questions.answerText: Because IRET restores three 16-bit values, SP increases by 6 overall.
questions.explanation: Because IRET restores three 16-bit values, SP increases by 6 overall.

questions.question: What does the 8086 CPU do immediately after receiving an INT instruction?
questions.answerText:
It saves FLAGS, CS, and IP on the stack, clears IF and TF, computes the vector address, and obtains the new IP
and CS values from the interrupt vector table.
questions.explanation:
It saves FLAGS, CS, and IP on the stack, clears IF and TF, computes the vector address, and obtains the new IP
and CS values from the interrupt vector table.

questions.question: How does the 8086 access the Interrupt Vector Table IVT, and why is the IVT necessary?
questions.answerText:
For interrupt type n, the vector address is n x 4. Four memory locations are reserved for each interrupt type in the
first 1 KB of memory. The IVT is necessary because it stores the address of the interrupt service routine for each
interrupt type.
questions.explanation:
For interrupt type n, the vector address is n x 4. Four memory locations are reserved for each interrupt type in the
first 1 KB of memory. The IVT is necessary because it stores the address of the interrupt service routine for each
interrupt type.

questions.question: What information is stored in the Interrupt Vector Table IVT?
questions.answerText:
For each interrupt type, four bytes are reserved. The first two bytes store the effective address to be loaded into
IP, and the next two bytes store the segment base address to be loaded into CS.
questions.explanation:
For each interrupt type, four bytes are reserved. The first two bytes store the effective address to be loaded into
IP, and the next two bytes store the segment base address to be loaded into CS.

questions.question: What specific operations are performed using the IVT when an INT instruction is executed?
questions.answerText:
The CPU multiplies the interrupt type number by 4 to get the vector address, reads the first word into IP, and
reads the next word into CS. Execution then continues from that CS:IP location.
questions.explanation:
The CPU multiplies the interrupt type number by 4 to get the vector address, reads the first word into IP, and
reads the next word into CS. Execution then continues from that CS:IP location.

questions.question: How does the 8086 switch execution to the Interrupt Service Routine ISR?
questions.answerText:
After saving FLAGS, CS, and IP, the processor loads IP and CS from the vector entry corresponding to the
interrupt type. That new CS:IP identifies the ISR entry point.
questions.explanation:
After saving FLAGS, CS, and IP, the processor loads IP and CS from the vector entry corresponding to the
interrupt type. That new CS:IP identifies the ISR entry point.

questions.question: What is the IRET instruction?
questions.answerText: IRET is the interrupt-return instruction used at the end of an ISR. It restores IP, CS, and flags from the stack.
questions.explanation: IRET is the interrupt-return instruction used at the end of an ISR. It restores IP, CS, and flags from the stack.

questions.question: After the execution of the ISR, how does the CPU return to the main program?
questions.answerText:
The ISR ends with IRET. IRET pops the saved IP, CS, and flag register values from the stack, increasing SP by 2
after each pop. The original program context is therefore restored.
questions.explanation:
The ISR ends with IRET. IRET pops the saved IP, CS, and flag register values from the stack, increasing SP by 2
after each pop. The original program context is therefore restored.

questions.question: What is a shift instruction in the 8086 microprocessor?
questions.answerText:
A shift instruction moves every bit of a register or memory operand one or more positions to the left or right.
During the shift, a bit is moved into the Carry Flag and a new bit position is filled according to the type of shift.
questions.explanation:
A shift instruction moves every bit of a register or memory operand one or more positions to the left or right.
During the shift, a bit is moved into the Carry Flag and a new bit position is filled according to the type of shift.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Logical Shift (SHL/SHR) and an Arithmetic Shift (SAL/SAR)?
questions.answerText:
For left shift, SHL and SAL are functionally identical: bits move left, the old most significant bit goes to CF, and
zero enters the least significant bit. SHR is logical right shift: zero enters the most significant bit. SAR is arithmetic
right shift: the sign bit is copied into the most significant bit so the sign is preserved.
questions.explanation:
For left shift, SHL and SAL are functionally identical: bits move left, the old most significant bit goes to CF, and
zero enters the least significant bit. SHR is logical right shift: zero enters the most significant bit. SAR is arithmetic
right shift: the sign bit is copied into the most significant bit so the sign is preserved.

questions.question: Which register is used to specify a multi-bit count shift operation?
questions.answerText: The CL register is used to specify the count for a multi-bit shift or rotate operation.
questions.explanation: The CL register is used to specify the count for a multi-bit shift or rotate operation.

questions.question: What is the maximum count value allowed in the CL register for shift operations?
questions.answerText:
The notes specify a count range of 1 to 255 when CL is used. Therefore the maximum count stated in the notes is
255 decimal.
questions.explanation:
The notes specify a count range of 1 to 255 when CL is used. Therefore the maximum count stated in the notes is
255 decimal.

questions.question:
Can a shift instruction use an immediate value like 3 directly, for example SHL AX, 3? If not, what
are the only two valid ways to specify the count?
questions.answerText:
According to the instruction forms shown in the notes, the count is specified either as 1 or through the CL register.
So the two forms are SHL/SAL operand,1 and SHL/SAL operand,CL. An immediate count such as 3 is not listed
as a valid 8086 form.
questions.explanation:
According to the instruction forms shown in the notes, the count is specified either as 1 or through the CL register.
So the two forms are SHL/SAL operand,1 and SHL/SAL operand,CL. An immediate count such as 3 is not listed
as a valid 8086 form.

questions.question: How does the SHL instruction work? What enters the LSB, and where does the shifted MSB go?
questions.answerText:
All bits move one position to the left. The old MSB is shifted into CF, and 0 enters the LSB. For multiple shifts
using CL, this operation is repeated for the specified count.
questions.explanation:
All bits move one position to the left. The old MSB is shifted into CF, and 0 enters the LSB. For multiple shifts
using CL, this operation is repeated for the specified count.

questions.question: How does the SHR instruction work? What enters the MSB, and where does the shifted LSB go?
questions.answerText: All bits move one position to the right. The old LSB is shifted into CF, and 0 enters the MSB.
questions.explanation: All bits move one position to the right. The old LSB is shifted into CF, and 0 enters the MSB.

questions.question: How does the SAR instruction work? Why is the MSB sign bit preserved during SAR?
questions.answerText:
All bits move one position to the right. The old LSB is shifted into CF, while the old MSB is retained in the MSB
position. Because the sign bit is copied rather than replaced by zero, the sign of a signed two’s-complement value
is preserved.
questions.explanation:
All bits move one position to the right. The old LSB is shifted into CF, while the old MSB is retained in the MSB
position. Because the sign bit is copied rather than replaced by zero, the sign of a signed two’s-complement value
is preserved.

questions.question: Why are SHL and SAL functionally identical in execution?
questions.answerText:
The notes list SHL and SAL as alternative names for the same left-shift operation: the operand shifts left, the old
MSB goes to CF, and zero enters the LSB.
questions.explanation:
The notes list SHL and SAL as alternative names for the same left-shift operation: the operand shifts left, the old
MSB goes to CF, and zero enters the LSB.

questions.question: How can SHL be used to perform fast multiplication by powers of 2?
questions.answerText:
Each left shift moves the binary point-equivalent position by one place and therefore corresponds to multiplying
the bit pattern by 2 when overflow is ignored. Repeated left shifts can therefore be used for multiplication by 2, 4,
8, and other powers of 2.
questions.explanation:
Each left shift moves the binary point-equivalent position by one place and therefore corresponds to multiplying
the bit pattern by 2 when overflow is ignored. Repeated left shifts can therefore be used for multiplication by 2, 4,
8, and other powers of 2.

questions.question: How can SAR be used to perform fast division of signed numbers by powers of 2?
questions.answerText:
SAR shifts a signed value right while preserving the sign bit. Therefore repeated SAR operations can be used as
a fast right-shift division technique for signed binary values, with the discarded low-order bits lost during the shift.

8086 Mid-Sem Answer Pack - grounded in the supplied 128-page notes
questions.explanation:
SAR shifts a signed value right while preserving the sign bit. Therefore repeated SAR operations can be used as
a fast right-shift division technique for signed binary values, with the discarded low-order bits lost during the shift.

8086 Mid-Sem Answer Pack - grounded in the supplied 128-page notes

questions.question: Why is SHR unsuitable for performing division on signed negative numbers?
questions.answerText:
SHR always inserts 0 into the MSB. A negative two’s-complement number has a 1 in its sign bit, so replacing that
bit with 0 does not preserve the negative sign. SAR is the arithmetic right shift intended to retain the sign bit.
questions.explanation:
SHR always inserts 0 into the MSB. A negative two’s-complement number has a 1 in its sign bit, so replacing that
bit with 0 does not preserve the negative sign. SAR is the arithmetic right shift intended to retain the sign bit.

questions.question: What happens to precision or data when shifting an odd number right using SHR or SAR?
questions.answerText:
The LSB is shifted out and placed into CF, so that bit of the original data is no longer part of the operand. Thus
one bit of information is discarded on each right shift.
questions.explanation:
The LSB is shifted out and placed into CF, so that bit of the original data is no longer part of the operand. Thus
one bit of information is discarded on each right shift.

questions.question: What is a rotate instruction, and how does it differ from a shift instruction?
questions.answerText:
A rotate operation circulates the bit pattern instead of inserting a new zero or sign bit. In a shift, a bit is discarded
and a new bit enters. In a rotate, the shifted-out bit is fed back into the operand or through CF.
questions.explanation:
A rotate operation circulates the bit pattern instead of inserting a new zero or sign bit. In a shift, a bit is discarded
and a new bit enters. In a rotate, the shifted-out bit is fed back into the operand or through CF.

questions.question: What are simple rotate instructions ROL and ROR?
questions.answerText:
ROL rotates the operand left and feeds the old MSB into the LSB; the old MSB is also copied to CF. ROR rotates
the operand right and feeds the old LSB into the MSB; the old LSB is also copied to CF.
questions.explanation:
ROL rotates the operand left and feeds the old MSB into the LSB; the old MSB is also copied to CF. ROR rotates
the operand right and feeds the old LSB into the MSB; the old LSB is also copied to CF.

questions.question: What are rotate-through-carry instructions RCL and RCR?
questions.answerText:
RCL rotates left through the Carry Flag. The old MSB goes to CF and the old CF enters the LSB. RCR rotates
right through CF. The old LSB goes to CF and the old CF enters the MSB.
questions.explanation:
RCL rotates left through the Carry Flag. The old MSB goes to CF and the old CF enters the LSB. RCR rotates
right through CF. The old LSB goes to CF and the old CF enters the MSB.

questions.question: In ROL, what happens to the MSB as it is shifted out?
questions.answerText: The old MSB is moved into the LSB and is also copied into CF.
questions.explanation: The old MSB is moved into the LSB and is also copied into CF.

questions.question: In ROR, what happens to the LSB as it is shifted out?
questions.answerText: The old LSB is moved into the MSB and is also copied into CF.
questions.explanation: The old LSB is moved into the MSB and is also copied into CF.

questions.question: In ROL, where does the MSB go? In RCL, where does the MSB go, and where does the old Carry
questions.answerText:
Flag go?
In ROL, the old MSB goes to the LSB and to CF. In RCL, the old MSB goes to CF, while the old CF goes into the
LSB.
questions.explanation:
Flag go?
In ROL, the old MSB goes to the LSB and to CF. In RCL, the old MSB goes to CF, while the old CF goes into the
LSB.

questions.question: How does RCL use the Carry Flag CF as a 9-bit or 17-bit register extension?
questions.answerText:
The notes show that RCL moves the old MSB into CF while the old CF enters the LSB. Thus the operand bits and
CF participate in one circular path. For an 8-bit operand this forms a 9-bit rotation path; for a 16-bit operand it
forms a 17-bit path.
questions.explanation:
The notes show that RCL moves the old MSB into CF while the old CF enters the LSB. Thus the operand bits and
CF participate in one circular path. For an 8-bit operand this forms a 9-bit rotation path; for a 16-bit operand it
forms a 17-bit path.

questions.question: How does RCR use the Carry Flag CF as a 9-bit or 17-bit register extension?
questions.answerText:
The notes show that RCR moves the old LSB into CF while the old CF enters the MSB. Hence the operand and
CF form one circular path: 9 bits for an 8-bit operand and 17 bits for a 16-bit operand.
questions.explanation:
The notes show that RCR moves the old LSB into CF while the old CF enters the MSB. Hence the operand and
CF form one circular path: 9 bits for an 8-bit operand and 17 bits for a 16-bit operand.

questions.question: What is the practical purpose of RCL and RCR in multi-byte or multi-word arithmetic operations?
questions.answerText:
Because CF participates in the rotation, RCL and RCR allow a carry or borrow-related bit to move between
adjacent word or byte portions. This makes them useful when propagating bit information across multi-byte or
multi-word arithmetic operations.
questions.explanation:
Because CF participates in the rotation, RCL and RCR allow a carry or borrow-related bit to move between
adjacent word or byte portions. This makes them useful when propagating bit information across multi-byte or
multi-word arithmetic operations.

questions.question: Which status flags are modified by shift and rotate instructions?
questions.answerText:
The notes distinguish them as follows. For SHL/SAL, SHR, and SAR, CF, OF, SF, ZF, and PF are altered, while
AF is shown as undefined. For ROL, ROR, RCL, and RCR, CF and OF are altered; SF, ZF, AF, and PF are not
altered.
questions.explanation:
The notes distinguish them as follows. For SHL/SAL, SHR, and SAR, CF, OF, SF, ZF, and PF are altered, while
AF is shown as undefined. For ROL, ROR, RCL, and RCR, CF and OF are altered; SF, ZF, AF, and PF are not
altered.

questions.question: What does the Carry Flag CF hold after a shift or rotate operation completes?
questions.answerText:
CF holds the last bit shifted or rotated out of the operand. For a left shift this is the old MSB; for a right shift this is
the old LSB. For RCL/RCR, CF receives the bit specified by the rotate-through-carry rule.
questions.explanation:
CF holds the last bit shifted or rotated out of the operand. For a left shift this is the old MSB; for a right shift this is
the old LSB. For RCL/RCR, CF receives the bit specified by the rotate-through-carry rule.

questions.question:
When the shift or rotate count is exactly 1, what does the Overflow Flag OF indicate?

8086 Mid-Sem Answer Pack - grounded in the supplied 128-page notes
questions.answerText:
The 128-page notes supplied here do not state the exact bit-level rule for interpreting OF for a single shift or rotate
count. They only record in the flag table that OF is altered by these instructions. Therefore this specific rule is not
stated in the source notes and is not invented here.
questions.explanation:
The 128-page notes supplied here do not state the exact bit-level rule for interpreting OF for a single shift or rotate
count. They only record in the flag table that OF is altered by these instructions. Therefore this specific rule is not

questions.question: Why is the value of OF undefined when the shift or rotate count is greater than 1?
questions.answerText:
The supplied notes do not explicitly give a rule explaining the undefined meaning of OF for counts greater than 1.
They provide the flag-impact table but do not state the count-dependent OF formula. Therefore the exact
explanation is not available in the source notes.
questions.explanation:
The supplied notes do not explicitly give a rule explaining the undefined meaning of OF for counts greater than 1.
They provide the flag-impact table but do not state the count-dependent OF formula. Therefore the exact
explanation is not available in the source notes.

questions.question: Which flags are left undefined or not modified after shift and rotate operations?
questions.answerText:
From the notes: for shift instructions, AF is marked undefined. For rotate instructions, SF, ZF, AF, and PF are not
altered; only CF and OF are altered. The notes therefore distinguish undefined from not modified rather than
treating them as the same.
questions.explanation:
From the notes: for shift instructions, AF is marked undefined. For rotate instructions, SF, ZF, AF, and PF are not
altered; only CF and OF are altered. The notes therefore distinguish undefined from not modified rather than
treating them as the same.

questions.question: Which segments are used in string instructions?
questions.answerText:
The notes use the Data Segment for source string data and the Extra Segment for destination string data. LODS
reads from DS, while STOS writes to ES. MOVS and CMPS use DS for the source and ES for the destination.
SCAS uses ES for the string being scanned.
questions.explanation:
The notes use the Data Segment for source string data and the Extra Segment for destination string data. LODS
reads from DS, while STOS writes to ES. MOVS and CMPS use DS for the source and ES for the destination.
SCAS uses ES for the string being scanned.

questions.question:
Which segment registers and associated index or pointer registers are used in string
instructions?
questions.answerText:
SI holds the source effective address and is associated with DS. DI holds the destination effective address and is
associated with ES. The accumulator is involved for LODS and STOS: LODSB/LODSW load AL/AX, while
STOSB/STOSW store AL/AX.
questions.explanation:
SI holds the source effective address and is associated with DS. DI holds the destination effective address and is
associated with ES. The accumulator is involved for LODS and STOS: LODSB/LODSW load AL/AX, while
STOSB/STOSW store AL/AX.

questions.question: What is the Direction Flag DF?
questions.answerText:
DF controls the direction in which SI and DI are automatically updated after a string instruction. DF = 0 means
increment; DF = 1 means decrement.
questions.explanation:
DF controls the direction in which SI and DI are automatically updated after a string instruction. DF = 0 means
increment; DF = 1 means decrement.

questions.question: Which instructions are used to set and clear the DF flag?
questions.answerText: CLD clears DF to 0. STD sets DF to 1.
questions.explanation: CLD clears DF to 0. STD sets DF to 1.

questions.question: Why is it necessary to set and clear the DF flag?
questions.answerText:
The DF determines whether string pointers move forward or backward through memory. It must be set or cleared
according to the direction in which the string data has to be processed.
questions.explanation:
The DF determines whether string pointers move forward or backward through memory. It must be set or cleared
according to the direction in which the string data has to be processed.

questions.question: What happens during string instruction execution when DF = 1?
questions.answerText:
The index registers are decremented after the operation. For byte operations SI and DI change by 1; for word
operations they change by 2.
questions.explanation:
The index registers are decremented after the operation. For byte operations SI and DI change by 1; for word
operations they change by 2.

questions.question: What happens during string instruction execution when DF = 0?
questions.answerText:
The index registers are incremented after the operation. For byte operations SI and DI change by 1; for word
operations they change by 2.
questions.explanation:
The index registers are incremented after the operation. For byte operations SI and DI change by 1; for word
operations they change by 2.

questions.question: What are repeat prefixes REP, REPE/REPZ, REPNE/REPNZ?
questions.answerText:
REP is a prefix used to repeat a string instruction. REPE and REPZ are equivalent names for repeat while equal,
and REPNZ and REPNE are equivalent names for repeat while not equal. The comparison-based forms use CX
together with the Zero Flag.
questions.explanation:
REP is a prefix used to repeat a string instruction. REPE and REPZ are equivalent names for repeat while equal,
and REPNZ and REPNE are equivalent names for repeat while not equal. The comparison-based forms use CX
together with the Zero Flag.

questions.question: Which register is used as the loop counter for repeat prefixes?
questions.answerText:
CX is the repetition counter. It is decremented by 1 after each execution of the string instruction under the repeat
prefix.
questions.explanation:
CX is the repetition counter. It is decremented by 1 after each execution of the string instruction under the repeat
prefix.

questions.question: How does REP work with MOVSB and STOSB?
questions.answerText:
With a plain REP prefix, the string instruction is repeated while CX is not zero. CX is decremented after each
execution. Thus REP MOVSB copies a sequence of bytes from DS:SI to ES:DI, while REP STOSB stores AL
repeatedly into ES:DI.
questions.explanation:
With a plain REP prefix, the string instruction is repeated while CX is not zero. CX is decremented after each
execution. Thus REP MOVSB copies a sequence of bytes from DS:SI to ES:DI, while REP STOSB stores AL
repeatedly into ES:DI.

questions.question: What is the difference between REPE and REPNE?
questions.answerText:
REPE/REPZ repeats while CX is not zero and ZF = 1. REPNZ/REPNE repeats while CX is not zero and ZF = 0.
The repeat terminates when either the CX condition or the required ZF condition becomes false.

questions.question: Which status flag is checked by REPE and REPNE during termination?
questions.answerText: The Zero Flag, ZF, is checked. REPE/REPZ requires ZF = 1; REPNZ/REPNE requires ZF = 0.
questions.explanation: The Zero Flag, ZF, is checked. REPE/REPZ requires ZF = 1; REPNZ/REPNE requires ZF = 0.

questions.question:
How do LODSB/LODSW and STOSB/STOSW work? Which segment registers and associated
registers are used?
questions.answerText:
LODS reads string data from the Data Segment using DS:SI and places one byte into AL or one word into AX. SI
is then incremented or decremented according to DF. STOS writes AL or AX to the Extra Segment using ES:DI,
and DI is then incremented or decremented according to DF.
questions.explanation:
LODS reads string data from the Data Segment using DS:SI and places one byte into AL or one word into AX. SI
is then incremented or decremented according to DF. STOS writes AL or AX to the Extra Segment using ES:DI,
and DI is then incremented or decremented according to DF.

questions.question: How do MOVSB/MOVSW work? Which segment registers and associated registers are used?
questions.answerText:
MOVSB copies one byte from DS:SI to ES:DI. MOVSW copies one word from DS:SI to ES:DI. Afterward SI and
DI are automatically updated according to DF: by 1 for byte operations and by 2 for word operations.
questions.explanation:
MOVSB copies one byte from DS:SI to ES:DI. MOVSW copies one word from DS:SI to ES:DI. Afterward SI and
DI are automatically updated according to DF: by 1 for byte operations and by 2 for word operations.

questions.question:
What is the difference between executing combined LODSB and STOSB instructions versus a
single MOVSB instruction?
questions.answerText:
LODSB first loads the source byte from DS:SI into AL, and STOSB then stores AL to ES:DI. MOVSB performs the
memory-to-memory string move directly from DS:SI to ES:DI. Therefore the LODSB + STOSB sequence uses the
accumulator as an intermediate step, whereas MOVSB transfers the byte directly between the two string memory
locations.
questions.explanation:
LODSB first loads the source byte from DS:SI into AL, and STOSB then stores AL to ES:DI. MOVSB performs the
memory-to-memory string move directly from DS:SI to ES:DI. Therefore the LODSB + STOSB sequence uses the
accumulator as an intermediate step, whereas MOVSB transfers the byte directly between the two string memory
locations.

questions.question:
How do CMPSB/CMPSW instructions work? Which segment registers and associated registers
are used?
questions.answerText:
CMPSB compares one byte from DS:SI with one byte from ES:DI by subtraction and uses the result to modify
flags. CMPSW does the same for one word. SI and DI are then automatically updated according to DF.
questions.explanation:
CMPSB compares one byte from DS:SI with one byte from ES:DI by subtraction and uses the result to modify
flags. CMPSW does the same for one word. SI and DI are then automatically updated according to DF.

questions.question:
How do SCASB/SCASW instructions work? Which segment registers and associated registers
are used?
questions.answerText:
SCASB compares AL with the byte at ES:DI by subtraction and modifies the flags. SCASW compares AX with the
word at ES:DI. DI is automatically incremented or decremented according to DF.
questions.explanation:
SCASB compares AL with the byte at ES:DI by subtraction and modifies the flags. SCASW compares AX with the
word at ES:DI. DI is automatically incremented or decremented according to DF.
